Rejoicing
ree-JOY-sing
n.
From rejoice + -ing; rejoice from Old French rejouir, “to gladden,” from Latin re- + gaudere (to be glad). Renders the Greek kauchēma, “ground or matter of boasting/rejoicing,” and chara, “joy”; and the Hebrew gīlāh, “rejoicing,” and simchah, “joy.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Rejoicing is the active habitual expression of the joy that grace has produced in the regenerate soul—not the occasional spike of happy circumstance, but the sustained outgoing of a heart that has found in Christ its supreme treasure and now overflows in praise, gladness, thanksgiving, and even boasting in the Lord. The verb of Philippians is its keynote: rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. The doubling is significant. Paul commands rejoicing not as an emotional state the saint manages to feel but as an act of obedience the saint performs: he rejoices, deliberately, in the Lord, always, even in the Roman imprisonment from which he writes. The grounds of biblical rejoicing are objective: in this ye greatly rejoice—Peter writes—though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: That the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ; the rejoicing is anchored in the inheritance reserved in heaven, the salvation ready to be revealed, the trial that perfects faith. Romans 5 names a triple ground of rejoicing: rejoicing in hope of the glory of God, rejoicing in tribulations (because they work patience, experience, hope), and rejoicing in God Himself, through whom we have received the atonement. Paul speaks of my joy and crown, my rejoicing in the Lord, and even I rejoice in the day of Christ. The Beatitude commands rejoicing in persecution: rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven. Habakkuk’s great closing line is rejoicing’s most extreme test: although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines... yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. Rejoicing is therefore the saint’s habitual register, anchored in the unchanging objective grounds the gospel supplies, sustained as an act of obedience even when feelings flag, and present even in tribulation because its sources are not the circumstances but the Lord Himself, the inheritance kept in heaven, and the Christ in whom both have been given.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines REJOICING as the act of expressing joy or gladness; the experience of joy or gladness; in scripture, the boasting or glorying which is the proper expression of the saint’s joy in the Lord.

expand to see more

REJOICING, n. — 1. The act of expressing joy or gladness. 2. The experience of joy or gladness. 3. The subject or cause of joy.

REJOICE, v.i. — To experience joy and gladness in a high degree; to be exhilarated with lively and pleasurable sensations; to exult. Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice (Phil 4:4).

📖 Key Scripture

Philippians 4:4 — "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice."

1 Thessalonians 5:16 — "Rejoice evermore."

Romans 5:2-3 — "By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also..."

Habakkuk 3:17-18 — "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines... yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Rejoicing is corrupted by the circumstance-dependent register of contemporary faith that rejoices when things go well and falls silent when they do not—and by the manufactured emotional register of certain worship traditions that produces a performance of rejoicing whose intensity has been engineered by music and atmosphere rather than wrought by the gospel.

expand to see more

Circumstance-dependent rejoicing is the most common contemporary corruption. The believer rejoices visibly when finances are abundant, health is good, family is intact, the church is growing—and falls silent or grumbles when any of these are removed or reduced. The biblical command is sharper. Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice—and Paul writes this from prison. Rejoice evermore—the apostle commands continual rejoicing without circumstantial qualification. Although the fig tree shall not blossom... Habakkuk takes rejoicing to its most extreme test, the loss of every visible provision, and concludes with a rejoicing that has nothing left to rejoice in but the LORD Himself. Recover the doctrine, and rejoicing recovers its anchorage: not in what is happening to me but in what God has done in Christ, what He has reserved for me, and what He Himself is. The objective grounds do not change with the circumstances; the rejoicing therefore need not change either.

The opposite corruption is the manufactured emotional rejoicing of certain worship traditions, in which the felt-intensity of rejoicing is engineered by music, lighting, atmosphere, and crowd dynamics rather than wrought by the gospel itself. The believer leaves such services emotionally lifted and identifies the lift with rejoicing in the Lord; the engineering is not the same thing. Biblical rejoicing is wrought by the gospel: the truth of what God has done in Christ pressed home to the soul produces a joy that is its proper response, and that joy expresses itself in rejoicing whether musical accompaniment is intense or absent. The recovery is the recovery of the substance: keep the gospel central in worship, preach Christ, lift up the cross, set forth the inheritance, name the grounds of joy—and the rejoicing that responds will be the rejoicing the Bible commands, anchored in what cannot be taken away.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kauchēma (ground/matter of rejoicing or boasting) and chara (joy); Hebrew gīlāh (rejoicing) and simchah (joy)—the saint’s habitual outgoing of gospel-wrought joy in the Lord, anchored in unchanging objective grounds.

expand to see more

Greek chairō (G5463) — to rejoice, be glad (Phil 4:4; 1 Thess 5:16).

Greek kauchēma (G2745) — ground or matter of rejoicing/boasting (Phil 1:26; Heb 3:6).

Greek chara (G5479) — joy, gladness (the noun).

Hebrew gīlāh (H1525) — rejoicing, gladness; cousin of simchah (joy).

Usage

"Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice—Paul writes from a Roman prison; the doubling is deliberate."

"Rejoicing is anchored in objective grounds—what God has done in Christ, what He has reserved, and what He Himself is—not in shifting circumstances."

"Habakkuk’s closing rejoicing is the verb’s most extreme test: every visible provision removed, the saint still rejoices in the LORD."
